name: Frederic Bastiat: the journalist-economist from Bayonne
scope: The T1/T2 foundational anchor for the Bastiat pillar: WHO the man was, before any of his arguments. T1: Frederic Bastiat (1801-1850) was a French classical-liberal economist, journalist, and statesman from the town of Mugron in the Landes region of southwestern France (near Bayonne). Trained as a merchant, he ran his grandfather's farm and read Adam Smith, Jean-Baptiste Say, and the English classical liberals on his own. T2: he wrote in the 1840s for the Journal des Economistes and founded a free-trade association modeled on Richard Cobden's Anti-Corn Law League; his prose is famously PLAIN -- he wrote so that a shopkeeper or a farmer could follow the argument, deliberately AVOIDING the mathematical style of continental economics. T3: elected to the French Constituent Assembly in 1848 after the February Revolution, then re-elected to the Legislative Assembly in 1849, sitting on the finance committee; he argued in the Chamber against protective tariffs, against the socialist proposals of Louis Blanc, and against paper-money schemes. T4: his best-known works appeared in a burst at the end of his life -- Economic Sophisms (Sophismes economiques, 1845 and 1848), That Which is Seen and That Which is Not Seen (Ce qu'on voit et ce qu'on ne voit pas, July 1850), and The Law (La Loi, June 1850) -- all written while he was dying of tuberculosis. T5: he traveled to Rome in the autumn of 1850 hoping the climate would help him breathe; his positive treatise Economic Harmonies (Harmonies economiques) was going to press incomplete when he died in Rome on December 24, 1850, aged 49. His famous last word, whispered to a friend at the bedside, is reported as 'la verite' (the truth) -- CORROBORATE AT BUILD.
source: PRIMARY: Bastiat's collected works (Liberty Fund edition, The Collected Works of Frederic Bastiat, 6 vols to date, 2011-). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Frederic Bastiat' (browser, 2026-09-05) -- birth Mugron 1801, death Rome December 24 1850, election to the Constituent Assembly 1848 and Legislative Assembly 1849, finance-committee service, Journal des Economistes writing, Anti-Corn Law inspiration, plain-prose style; Grokipedia 'Journal des Economistes' for the periodical context. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: exact birthdate (June 30 1801), the wording of the reported 'la verite' last word.
framing_note: The teach-before-test T1/T2 anchor for the whole pillar -- every downstream Bastiat ladder can safely name him because THIS ladder plants him. Dinner-test payoff: T5 (dying at 49 of tuberculosis in Rome, correcting page proofs of his one positive treatise) and T2 (deliberately writing plain so a shopkeeper could follow, against the mathematical continental style). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: if the stem says he sat on the finance committee in 1849, the answer is NOT 'he was a legislator' -- it is the specific move he made there (opposing Louis Blanc's socialist scheme, or opposing a specific tariff). DISTRACTOR MINE: other 19th-century French economists (Jean-Baptiste Say, Michel Chevalier, Gustave de Molinari, Yves Guyot), other British free-traders of the era (Cobden, Bright, John Bright's brother Jacob), other free-trade leagues (the Anti-Corn Law League itself, the Cobden Club), other reasons for his early death (a distractor should be a real 19th-century wasting disease). name: 1840s France: the socialists Bastiat was answering
scope: The OPPONENTS ladder: the specific French socialist and protectionist arguments Bastiat was writing against, so the pupil can hear the other side of every debate. T1: France in the 1840s is not yet industrial like Britain; the July Monarchy (Louis-Philippe, 1830-48) protects domestic ironmasters and textile-makers with heavy tariffs, and food is expensive because grain imports are restricted. T2: LOUIS BLANC (1811-1882) is the leading 'socialist of the state' -- his 1839 book The Organization of Labor (L'Organisation du travail) demands government-funded 'social workshops' (ateliers sociaux) where the state guarantees every worker a job and equal wages; after the February 1848 Revolution he actually gets to try it as a member of the Provisional Government. T3: the National Workshops (Ateliers nationaux) open in Paris in February 1848 and enroll over 100,000 unemployed men within weeks; the treasury cannot pay them for real work, wages become a straight welfare payment, the scheme is closed in June 1848 and the June Days uprising follows (thousands killed). T4: PIERRE-JOSEPH PROUDHON (1809-1865), the mutualist anarchist, argues in What Is Property? (1840) that 'property is theft' (la propriete, c'est le vol) and pushes for a Bank of the People (Banque du peuple) issuing INTEREST-FREE credit (credit gratuit) -- Bastiat spends fourteen letters in Le Voix du Peuple (October 1849-March 1850) debating him, defending interest as the market price of time-preference. T5: at the same time the protectionists in the Chamber -- led by figures around Adolphe Thiers -- defend high tariffs as 'protecting French labor'; Bastiat's Economic Sophisms (1845, 1848) is a satirical field guide to their arguments, and the Petition of the Candlemakers is the sharpest single satire. Further rungs: SAINT-SIMON (Claude-Henri, 1760-1825) and CHARLES FOURIER (1772-1837) as the earlier utopian-socialist generation whose ideas the 1848ers were trying to implement; Karl Marx's Communist Manifesto also published February 1848 in London (different tradition, same moment).

CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Bastiat-Proudhon debate' for the 1849-50 credit-gratuit exchange in La Voix du Peuple; Grokipedia 'Economic Sophisms' for the 1845 and 1848 collections. PRIMARY (for downstream ladders): Bastiat's Free Trade and Other Fundamental Issues (Liberty Fund CW vol 2) contains the Proudhon letters in English. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: exact enrollment figures for the National Workshops (100,000+ is the range in the standard sources), the exact date range of the Bastiat-Proudhon letters.
framing_note: The 'know your opponent' anchor -- lets the bank name Louis Blanc, Proudhon, and the National Workshops honestly in later ladders WITHOUT ambushing the kid. Dinner-test payoff: T3 (a real 1848 experiment that enrolled 100,000 unemployed men in a matter of weeks and collapsed in months, followed by a shooting uprising) and T4 (the anarchist Proudhon and the classical liberal Bastiat conducting an actual epistolary duel across a newspaper for six months). name: That Which is Seen and That Which is Not Seen: the founding essay
scope: The 1850 essay that founds the method. T1: in July 1850, dying of tuberculosis, Bastiat publishes a pamphlet titled Ce qu'on voit et ce qu'on ne voit pas -- 'That Which is Seen and That Which is Not Seen'. It runs about 60 pages and contains twelve short chapters, each a worked example. T2: the OPENING sentence sets the whole method: 'In the economic sphere, an act, a habit, an institution, a law produces not only one effect, but a series of effects. Of these effects, the first alone is immediate ... the other effects emerge only subsequently; THEY ARE NOT SEEN; we are fortunate if we FORESEE them.' T3: the difference between a bad economist and a good economist, Bastiat says, is just this: 'The bad economist confines himself to the visible effect; the good economist takes into account both the effect that can be seen and those effects that must be foreseen.' The whole rest of the essay is worked examples of this one move. T4: the twelve chapters cover -- the broken window, the disbanding of troops, taxes, theaters and fine arts, public works, the middleman, trade restrictions, machines, credit, Algeria, thrift and luxury, and the right to work. Each takes a policy that people cheer for its VISIBLE effect and traces the INVISIBLE effect the cheer ignores. T5: the essay's LATER reception is enormous: Henry Hazlitt's Economics in One Lesson (1946) is explicitly a book-length restatement of the method, dedicated to Bastiat; Milton Friedman calls it a formative influence; Thomas Sowell's 'compared to what?' and 'stage-one thinking vs stage-two thinking' are the same move renamed for the 20th century. Further rungs: the essay was NOT translated to English until W.B. Hodgson's 1859 version; the Liberty Fund's George B. de Huszar translation (1964, still standard) is the one Hazlitt was working from; the Foundation for Economic Education (FEE) has kept it continuously in print in America since 1946.

CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Parable of the broken window' and 'Frederic Bastiat' (browser, 2026-09-05) -- the July 1850 publication date, the twelve-chapter structure, the opening 'bad economist vs good economist' formulation, Hazlitt's 1946 dedication to Bastiat, FEE's stewardship. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (the exact opening sentence, which is the whole method in one paragraph) and T5 (a 1946 American book that is essentially the same essay in modern English, still selling). name: The broken window: the shopkeeper's son and the missing coat
scope: The most famous single paragraph in classical liberal economics. T1: chapter 1 of the 1850 essay opens on a scene -- 'Have you ever witnessed the anger of the good shopkeeper, James Goodfellow, when his careless SON has happened to break a pane of glass?' (Bastiat uses the placeholder name Jacques Bonhomme in the French; standard English renderings say 'James Goodfellow'). T2: the bystanders CONSOLE the shopkeeper with the argument that has become the fallacy's name: 'It is an ill wind that blows nobody good. Everybody must live, and what would become of the GLAZIERS if panes of glass were never broken?' The broken pane, they say, gives the glazier six FRANCS of business (Bastiat's specific number). T3: Bastiat's move -- 'It is not seen that as our shopkeeper has spent six francs upon one thing, he cannot spend them upon another.' The glazier's six-franc job is SEEN; what is UNSEEN is the SHOE, the BOOK, or (Bastiat's own example) the NEW COAT the shopkeeper would have bought from the tailor, which now he cannot. T4: the net accounting -- BEFORE the break, the shopkeeper had a window AND six francs; AFTER, he has only a window. The community as a whole is exactly one window POORER. The bystander's whole argument, Bastiat says, treats DESTRUCTION as PRODUCTION -- 'destruction is not profit.' T5: the modern applications the same essay implies and later thinkers spell out: Hurricane Katrina 'stimulating' the Gulf economy (Paul Krugman columns 2001 and 2011 famously arguing broken-window logic for war and disaster); World War II 'ending the Great Depression' (the SEEN is the wartime employment; the UNSEEN is the household consumption that fell 20%+ during the war); post-9/11 rebuilding as 'growth' (Krugman column September 14, 2001); Cash for Clunkers 2009 destroying 690,000 used cars (SEEN: 690,000 new-car sales; UNSEEN: 690,000 poor families who could no longer buy a $2,000 used car).
source: PRIMARY: Bastiat, 'Ce qu'on voit et ce qu'on ne voit pas', chapter I 'La vitre cassee' (Paris, July 1850); English 'The Broken Window' in Selected Essays (FEE, 1964, de Huszar tr.). name: The petition of the candlemakers: a law against the SUN
scope: The greatest satirical petition in the history of economics. T1: in 1845 Bastiat publishes in Economic Sophisms a mock petition addressed to the French Chamber of Deputies, on behalf of 'the Manufacturers of Candles, Waxlights, Lamps, Candlesticks, Street Lamps, Snuffers, Extinguishers, and the Producers of Oil, Tallow, Rosin, Alcohol, and, generally, of Everything Connected with Lighting.' Its title is 'Petition des fabricants de chandelles' -- the Petition of the Candlemakers. T2: the petition begs the Chamber for a law requiring the CLOSING of 'all windows, dormers, skylights, inside and outside shutters, curtains, casements, bull's-eyes, deadlights, and blinds' during daytime hours. T3: the reason: the candlemakers are suffering 'from the ruinous competition of a RIVAL who apparently works under conditions so far superior to our own for the production of light that he is FLOODING the domestic market with it at an incredibly LOW price.' The rival is named in the second paragraph: 'This rival is none other than THE SUN.' T4: the punch of the satire -- every argument the real protectionists in the Chamber were using for iron, coal, and textile tariffs is now made word-for-word for a tariff against the sun. If it is good to protect French labor from cheap foreign coal, why is it not good to protect them from FREE sunlight? Bastiat lists the industries that will 'benefit' downstream: tallow farmers (more cattle needed), whaling fleets (more oil), forests (more wood for extinguishers), the shipping trade -- exactly the multiplier arguments protectionists used for real tariffs. T5: the deep move -- the petition works as a REDUCTIO on the protectionist principle: if 'more expensive is better because it creates domestic jobs', then destroying free abundance is a POLICY GOAL. The candlemakers' petition and the negative-railway argument are two halves of the same reductio: one against tariffs (candlemakers), one against make-work schemes (negative railway). Further rungs: 'Petition of the Candlemakers' is now standard shorthand in economics writing for any argument that treats abundance as a THREAT and scarcity as a BENEFIT (Milton Friedman refers to it in Free to Choose; Don Boudreaux at Cafe Hayek has cited it in dozens of columns).

CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Candlemakers' petition' and 'Economic Sophisms' (browser, 2026-09-05) -- 1845 first-series publication, the industries-that-will-benefit list, the SUN as the named 'unfair competitor', its standard use as a protectionism-reductio. name: The negative railway: break every rail line to create jobs
scope: The second great reductio, aimed at make-work arguments. T1: in Economic Sophisms Bastiat imagines a proposed French railway from Paris to Madrid. T2: the deputy from BORDEAUX rises in the Chamber and points out that the traders of Bordeaux would benefit if the trains had to STOP at Bordeaux (rather than run straight through); therefore a break in the line at Bordeaux would generate work for Bordeaux porters, innkeepers, and warehousemen. T3: Bastiat's push -- if this is good, then the deputy from Angouleme should propose a break at Angouleme, and the deputy from Poitiers a break at Poitiers, and the deputy from Tours a break at Tours, and so on. T4: taken to its conclusion, the argument requires a break at EVERY station. But a railway that is broken at every station is not a railway at all -- it is just a series of unconnected roads. The 'jobs' argument, taken seriously, DESTROYS the very thing that made the jobs possible. T5: the modern applications -- the same reasoning was used to argue that MECHANIZATION 'destroys jobs' (looms destroy weaving jobs, tractors destroy farm jobs, computers destroy clerk jobs, AI destroys writing jobs); Bastiat's move is that if machines destroying jobs is bad, then we should also destroy the SPADE (which put people who dig with sticks out of work) and the WHEEL (which put people who drag loads on sledges out of work). The 'saved labor' is the seen; what is UNSEEN is what those same workers now do INSTEAD, and the goods now available at lower cost. Further rungs: the negative-railway argument is the twin of the broken-window fallacy -- broken window says destruction is not creation; negative railway says friction is not creation. Together they close both flanks of the make-work argument.

name: The Law: when legal force is used for plunder
scope: Bastiat's dying-year political treatise. T1: in June 1850, six months before his death, Bastiat publishes a pamphlet of about 75 pages titled La Loi -- 'The Law'. T2: the treatise's opening definition -- 'The law is the collective organization of the individual right to lawful defense.' Its legitimate function, Bastiat says, is only to defend the pre-existing individual rights that would exist even without law: LIFE, LIBERTY, and PROPERTY. T3: Bastiat's central diagnosis -- when the law is used INSTEAD to take from some people and give to others, it becomes what he calls LEGAL PLUNDER (spoliation legale). His test to detect legal plunder: 'See if the law takes from some persons what belongs to them, and gives it to other persons to whom it does not belong. See if the law benefits one citizen at the expense of another by doing what the citizen himself cannot do without committing a crime.' T4: the essay names two large categories of legal plunder in 1850 France: PROTECTIONISM (tariffs that transfer wealth from consumers to sheltered producers) and SOCIALISM (the National Workshops, guaranteed jobs, guaranteed credit -- transfers from taxpayers to the schemes' beneficiaries). Bastiat's blunt line: 'The state is the great fictitious entity by which everyone seeks to live at the expense of everyone else' (L'Etat, c'est la grande fiction a travers laquelle tout le monde s'efforce de vivre aux depens de tout le monde). T5: the essay's afterlife -- The Law is by a wide margin Bastiat's most-read work in English, kept continuously in print in America since FEE's 1950 edition; Ron Paul cites it in Liberty Defined (2011) as his single most-recommended economics text; the pamphlet is often the first Austrian-adjacent text libertarian teenagers read. Further rungs: the essay's warning against 'legal plunder' as CORRUPTING morally -- when legal force is used to take, people stop distinguishing right from wrong and start distinguishing legal from illegal.

name: Economic Sophisms: the wider satire collection
scope: The book of which the candlemakers and negative-railway pieces are only the two most famous chapters. T1: Sophismes economiques appeared in two SERIES -- First Series (Paris: Guillaumin, 1845, 22 short essays) and Second Series (Paris: Guillaumin, January 1848, 17 more essays). Together they form the essential Bastiat satirical corpus. T2: the FRAMING device runs through the collection -- Bastiat invents a common-sense French peasant named JACQUES BONHOMME who keeps encountering, and demolishing, the arguments of protectionists, tax-and-transfer schemers, and make-work advocates. Some essays are straight arguments, some are DIALOGUES between Bonhomme and a protectionist deputy, some are mock petitions like the candlemakers'. T3: representative chapters beyond the two famous ones -- 'Abundance and Scarcity' (why the goal is more goods at lower prices, not fewer at higher); 'Obstacles and Causes' (a clarification that human wants are 'obstacles' the economy overcomes, not 'causes' of prosperity); 'Effort and Result' (the seen-vs-unseen move applied to labor); 'The Two Axes' (a mayor forbids a woodcutter from using his sharp axe because it would put men with dull axes out of work); 'The Immediate Cause' (proximate vs deeper cause in economic reasoning). T4: the collection's translation history in English is important -- for a century the standard translation was Patrick James Stirling's 1873 English edition, retitled Economic Sophisms; the current standard is Jane Willems's Liberty Fund translation (CW vols 3, 2017), which restored many chapters and cleaned up 19th-century Britishisms. T5: the collection's REACH -- economists as varied as Milton Friedman, Thomas Sowell, Deirdre McCloskey, and Don Boudreaux all cite Economic Sophisms as formative; every serious classical-liberal reading list has it; the book's method of demolishing bad arguments THROUGH SATIRE (rather than technical formal analysis) is Bastiat's specific contribution to the tradition. Further rungs: some sophisms are aimed at LEFT arguments (make-work, guaranteed-jobs schemes) and some at RIGHT arguments (tariffs for domestic producers) -- Bastiat's move is the same in both directions, which is what makes the collection a METHOD text.

name: Economic Harmonies: Bastiat's positive theory
scope: The book Bastiat did not live to finish. T1: Bastiat's other works are DESTRUCTIVE -- they demolish bad arguments. Harmonies economiques (Paris: Guillaumin, 1850) was his one attempt at a POSITIVE, systematic theory of how a free economy actually generates cooperation and prosperity. T2: the book's central thesis is that human interests, in a free society, are naturally HARMONIOUS rather than antagonistic -- against the classical-economics view of Ricardo and (later) Marx that class interests are fundamentally OPPOSED. Bastiat argues that when exchange is voluntary, gains for one party do not require losses for another (Marx's key error, in Bastiat's frame). T3: the book introduces Bastiat's theory of VALUE -- value is created by the SERVICE rendered, not by the labor spent; a diamond found by chance in a stream and a diamond dug out at great labor have the same VALUE if they are equally useful to buyers (this anticipates the marginal revolution of Menger and Jevons twenty years later, though Bastiat did not have the marginal-analysis vocabulary). T4: the SEEN/UNSEEN method appears in a positive form -- everything a producer sells, someone else has chosen to buy voluntarily; the whole apparatus of prices is a communication system that lets millions of strangers coordinate without a central plan (anticipating Hayek's 1945 'Use of Knowledge in Society' by 95 years). T5: the book was published INCOMPLETE. Bastiat wrote ten chapters and had drafted portions of ten more when tuberculosis killed him in Rome on December 24, 1850. His friend Prosper Paillottet edited the fragments into a second, larger edition in 1851. Modern readers get the completed portion plus the fragments; the finished book Bastiat intended never existed. Further rungs: Joseph Schumpeter in his History of Economic Analysis (1954) called Bastiat a great pamphleteer but dismissed Harmonies as unfinished and second-rate; more recent Austrian scholarship (Salerno, Hulsmann, Thornton) has reappraised it upward, pointing to the subjectivist-value hints as genuinely ahead of their time.

name: Bastiat vs Proudhon: the 1849-50 debate on interest
scope: The great published duel between the classical liberal and the mutualist anarchist. T1: Pierre-Joseph Proudhon (1809-1865), the French anarchist who declared 'property is theft', argued in the late 1840s that CHARGING INTEREST on a loan was itself theft -- lenders extract wealth without labor. His proposed remedy: a Bank of the People (Banque du peuple) that would issue INTEREST-FREE credit (credit gratuit) to workers, breaking the power of capital. T2: Bastiat took Proudhon on directly in a public exchange of THIRTEEN letters (some sources say fourteen) in La Voix du Peuple (Proudhon's own paper) between October 1849 and March 1850 -- a nearly six-month debate carried out in front of Proudhon's own readership. T3: Bastiat's core argument was TIME-PREFERENCE (though he did not use that later term): a person who lends 1,000 francs for a year gives up the use of that money for a year; interest is not payment for the LABOR of lending but payment for the TIME the lender has done without his own capital. Free credit would eliminate not lending but the WILLINGNESS to lend -- savings would move into hoarding, and productive borrowers would find nothing to borrow. T4: Proudhon countered that Bastiat was confusing NATURAL and ARTIFICIAL scarcity; he pushed the point that in his ideal mutualist economy, banks would multiply, competing lenders would drive interest to zero organically, and no coercion would be needed. Bastiat pressed back: even in Proudhon's ideal, WHY WOULD ANYONE LEND at zero? T5: the debate ended without either side conceding, but Proudhon later called Bastiat 'the most vigorous of my adversaries' (le plus vigoureux de mes adversaires); modern Austrian economists (Bohm-Bawerk's Capital and Interest 1884-89, Mises's Human Action 1949) built the full time-preference theory on essentially Bastiat's foundations. Further rungs: the letters are collected in Bastiat's Free Credit / Gratuity of Credit (Liberty Fund CW vol 4); this is one of the few Bastiat texts NOT primarily satirical -- it is a careful sustained argument on capital theory.

name: Bastiat and Cobden: the Anti-Corn Law friendship
scope: The English inspiration and the personal friendship. T1: RICHARD COBDEN (1804-1865) and JOHN BRIGHT (1811-1889) led the Anti-Corn Law League in Britain, founded 1838-39 in Manchester, to repeal the British tariffs on imported grain (the Corn Laws, first passed 1815) that kept food expensive to protect landlord incomes. T2: after seven years of relentless public campaigning -- pamphlets, mass meetings, cheap-newspaper propaganda -- the League succeeded on June 25, 1846: Prime Minister Sir Robert Peel repealed the Corn Laws, splitting his own Conservative Party in the process. Peel resigned four days later; the repeal became the classic case study for a mass free-trade movement winning against a landed political interest. T3: Bastiat had been WATCHING the League from France. In the summer of 1845 he traveled to England expressly to meet Cobden and observe the League's methods; the two men became close friends and correspondents. Bastiat wrote a book, Cobden et la Ligue (Paris: Guillaumin, 1845), introducing the League's campaign to French readers and translating its speeches and pamphlets. T4: returning to France, Bastiat founded the French Free Trade Association (Association pour la liberte des echanges) in February 1846, deliberately modeled on the League; the association held rallies in Marseilles, Bordeaux, and Paris, published a periodical (Le Libre-Echange, from November 1846), and lobbied the Chamber for tariff reform. It never achieved the political breakthrough the British League did -- French protectionists were too entrenched, and the 1848 Revolution interrupted the movement. T5: the personal friendship lasted until Bastiat's death; the two men exchanged letters throughout 1846-1850 (the correspondence survives and is published in the Liberty Fund CW vol 1). When Bastiat died in Rome in December 1850, Cobden wrote a public tribute calling him 'the most illustrious of the Free-Traders on the Continent.' Further rungs: the Manchester School (Cobden, Bright, and their circle) as the British counterpart to Bastiat's tradition; John Bright's later career as a peace campaigner and cabinet minister; the Corn Law repeal as the definitive 19th-century case of an organized public campaign winning against a concentrated economic interest.

name: 'The state is the great fiction': the most famous Bastiat line
scope: One sentence that became a classical-liberal motto. T1: Bastiat first wrote the line in a short essay titled 'The State' (L'Etat) published in the Journal des Debats on September 25, 1848 -- during the same year he was serving in the Constituent Assembly. He re-used it in The Law (June 1850). T2: the sentence in French: 'L'Etat, c'est la grande fiction a travers laquelle tout le monde s'efforce de vivre aux depens de tout le monde.' Standard English (D. Russell tr.): 'The state is the great fictitious entity by which everyone seeks to live at the expense of everyone else.' T3: the CONTEXT -- Bastiat had just watched the 1848 Provisional Government promise a 'right to work' at guaranteed wages (via the National Workshops), promise cheap credit (via Proudhon-inspired schemes), promise support to arts and industries, promise pensions. Every promise sounded generous IN THE SEEN. Bastiat's line named the UNSEEN: none of it comes from nowhere; every gift to one voter is a taking from another. T4: the essay's opening frame is a mock definition contest -- Bastiat offers a prize to any reader who can give a coherent definition of 'the State' that does NOT reduce to 'the great fiction by which everyone tries to live at everyone else's expense.' He never had to pay out. T5: the line's afterlife -- it is quoted in nearly every modern classical-liberal writer (Hayek, Rothbard, Sowell, Buchanan, Ron Paul, Thomas Woods); it appears on FEE and Mises Institute banners, is the most-clipped Bastiat line in memes, and functions as a compact statement of the public-choice insight that would win Buchanan the Nobel Prize in 1986. Further rungs: the essay 'The State' is short (about 15 pages) and works well as a companion to The Law; it is the ONE Bastiat text most beginners have heard the punch line from without knowing the source.

name: 'Ineptly defended': the line Sowell borrowed
scope: A shorter Bastiat maxim that traveled through 20th-century economics. T1: in Economic Sophisms (1845-48), Bastiat writes: 'La pire chose qui puisse arriver a une bonne cause, ce n'est pas d'etre habilement attaquee, c'est d'etre mal defendue' -- 'The worst thing that can happen to a good cause is not to be skillfully attacked, but to be ineptly defended.' T2: the CONTEXT -- Bastiat had watched French classical liberals lose public arguments not because their opponents were persuasive but because their allies made the case badly (with abstract theory instead of specific examples, or with tribal defensiveness instead of engagement with the strongest form of the opposing argument). T3: the practical implication Bastiat drew -- the free-trade defender's job is to state the PROTECTIONIST case in its STRONGEST FORM, then answer it; anything less is inept defense that discredits the cause. Nearly every essay in Economic Sophisms follows this method -- Bastiat first states the protectionist argument fairly and even sympathetically, THEN dismantles it. T4: THOMAS SOWELL (born 1930), the 20th-century American economist, made 'address the strongest form of the argument' a signature move -- his Basic Economics (2000, now in a 5th edition), Knowledge and Decisions (1980), and A Conflict of Visions (1987) all steelman opposing views before critiquing them. Sowell cites Bastiat as a formative influence in his memoir A Personal Odyssey (2000). T5: the line is now a standard classical-liberal / rationalist motto for STEELMANNING (a term coined in 21st-century rationalist circles for stating an opposing argument in its strongest form before answering it). The RATIONALIST community (Scott Alexander, LessWrong, Effective Altruism circles c. 2010s) uses 'steelman' in essentially Bastiat's sense. Further rungs: the same discipline is a Karl Popper move (in The Open Society and Its Enemies 1945) and a John Stuart Mill move (in On Liberty 1859) -- there is a long liberal tradition of it; Bastiat's line just gave it a memorable name.

name: Hazlitt's Economics in One Lesson: Bastiat in American English
scope: The American 20th-century restatement. T1: HENRY HAZLITT (1894-1993) was an American journalist -- economics editor of The Nation, financial columnist for The New York Times (1934-46), and columnist for Newsweek (1946-66). He was largely SELF-TAUGHT, having left college early for financial reasons; he read Mises's Human Action (1949) in draft and became a lifelong friend and defender of Mises. T2: in 1946 Hazlitt published a short book, ECONOMICS IN ONE LESSON, explicitly dedicated to Bastiat and structured as a book-length restatement of the seen/unseen method for a mid-20th-century American reader. The book has never gone out of print (Harper & Brothers 1946, Arlington House 1979, various editions since); it has sold over 1 million copies. T3: the book's ONE LESSON, stated in chapter 1: 'The art of economics consists in looking not merely at the immediate but at the longer effects of any act or policy; it consists in tracing the consequences of that policy not merely for one group but for all groups.' The rest of the book applies this lesson to specific 1946 American policies. T4: the CHAPTERS cover -- public works (WPA, TVA), taxation, credit-diverting government projects, machines and unemployment, spread-the-work schemes, disbanding troops, government price-fixing, rent control (uniquely damaging), minimum wage laws, tariffs, export drives, 'parity' prices, saving the X industry, functionalism of pricing -- each is Bastiat's method applied to a specific New Deal or postwar American policy. T5: RECEPTION -- the book became the standard first classical-liberal / Austrian economics book for a generation of American libertarians; it is on Milton Friedman's recommended-reading lists, on Ron Paul's lists, on the Mises Institute's; John Chamberlain praised it in the Wall Street Journal; F.A. Hayek called it 'a brilliant performance.' Hazlitt himself co-founded the FEE (Foundation for Economic Education) with Leonard Read in 1946, the same year the book appeared. Further rungs: Hazlitt's other works include The Failure of the New Economics (1959, a chapter-by-chapter refutation of Keynes's General Theory) and Man vs. the Welfare State (1969); he stayed at Newsweek for 20 years as a lonely classical-liberal voice in mainstream American journalism.

name: FEE and the American rediscovery: Leonard Read, 1946
scope: How Bastiat came back into English print. T1: by the early 20th century Bastiat had faded from the standard economics-teaching canon; the two-volume 1873 Stirling English translation of his works was out of print and hard to find; American academics increasingly followed the German Historical School or (from the 1930s) the Keynesian mainstream. T2: LEONARD E. READ (1898-1983) was a former Los Angeles Chamber of Commerce executive who had become convinced by Mises's and Hayek's arguments that the American classical-liberal tradition needed institutional support. In March 1946 he founded the Foundation for Economic Education (FEE) in Irvington-on-Hudson, New York. T3: FEE's founding mission was to keep classical-liberal / free-market economic writing IN PRINT and ACCESSIBLE, at a time when the mainstream would not carry it. FEE re-published Bastiat's The Law (1950, translated by Dean Russell), Selected Essays on Political Economy (1964, edited by George B. de Huszar), and Economic Sophisms (1964); these translations were the standard American editions for the next 50 years. T4: FEE also published Hazlitt's Economics in One Lesson (though Harper was the original publisher), Read's own essay 'I, Pencil' (December 1958, in FEE's magazine The Freeman -- a first-person narrative by a pencil showing the millions of coordinated actions required to produce one, illustrating Hayek's knowledge-problem argument), and standing runs of Mises, Hayek, and later Rothbard. T5: FEE has continued into the 21st century as a classical-liberal educational institution (student seminars, online courses, the FEE.org site). Its critical function in the 1946-1970 window was that it was the ONE place in America where Bastiat's English texts stayed continuously in print; when Rothbard's Mises Institute was founded at Auburn in 1982, and later the Cato Institute (1977) and Reason Foundation (1968) grew, they built on FEE's foundational work of keeping the source texts available. Further rungs: FEE's 'I, Pencil' by Leonard Read is one of the most-anthologized short essays in classical-liberal writing -- Milton Friedman built the second episode of his 1980 Free to Choose television series around its argument.

name: Bastiat and slavery: the 1848 abolition vote
scope: One of Bastiat's clearest moral positions, sometimes muddled in secondary sources. T1: France ABOLISHED slavery in her colonies (Martinique, Guadeloupe, French Guiana, Reunion) by decree of the Second Republic's Provisional Government on April 27, 1848, championed by Victor SCHOELCHER as under-secretary of the Navy -- the second and definitive French abolition (an earlier 1794 abolition had been reversed by Napoleon in 1802). T2: Bastiat, elected to the Constituent Assembly for the Landes department in April 1848 (i.e. AFTER the abolition decree of April 27, since the Assembly first met on May 4), was on the record as a longstanding OPPONENT of slavery. He had already argued in Economic Sophisms and in his journalism that slavery was both morally intolerable and economically self-defeating (a slave has no incentive to be productive; slavery corrupts the master's character and distorts the whole economy of the slaveholding region). T3: in the Assembly he voted to SUPPORT the abolition and to fund compensation for the freed slaves' transition (a common late-1840s abolitionist framework -- the British abolition of 1833 had used compensated emancipation, controversially compensating the former slave owners rather than the freed slaves). T4: Bastiat's economic argument against slavery was Bastiat's usual seen/unseen and harmony-of-interests move -- the slave-owning region SEES the free labor and its exportable products; it does not see the population living without incentive, the free labor market strangled, the innovation frozen, the moral character of the master class ruined. Slavery, for Bastiat, is the maximal case of legal plunder (as later spelled out in The Law): one person's life labor is taken from them by legal force. T5: this puts Bastiat squarely with the abolitionist tradition -- with Wilberforce and the British Clapham Sect, with Schoelcher in France, with Frederick Douglass and William Lloyd Garrison in America. American classical liberals in the 19th century (Lysander Spooner, William Ellery Channing, later Bastiat-influenced Northern free-traders) drew on Bastiat's arguments. Further rungs: some 20th- and 21st-century secondary summaries have wrongly implied Bastiat was silent on slavery or ambivalent; the primary record (his Sophismes economiques essay 'Justice et fraternite', his Assembly speeches, his correspondence) makes the abolitionist position unambiguous.

name: Death in Rome, Christmas Eve 1850
scope: The end. T1: by the autumn of 1850 Bastiat's tuberculosis (which had troubled him for years) had become severe -- his voice was going, his throat was inflamed, he could barely eat. On the advice of doctors he traveled south to try the warmer Italian climate. T2: he arrived in ROME in September 1850, hoping the air would help him recover. He continued to work -- correcting page proofs of the first volume of Economic Harmonies and drafting further chapters -- from his sickroom. T3: his condition worsened through October and November; his final letters, some to Cobden in England, some to his French friends, are collected in the Liberty Fund CW vol 1 and are strikingly serene about the approaching end. He asked for reports on French politics and on the reception of his last pamphlets. T4: on December 24, 1850 -- CHRISTMAS EVE -- Frederic Bastiat died in Rome, aged 49. His last reported word, according to friends at the bedside, was 'la verite' -- 'the truth' -- though this is a reported detail and biographies vary on exact wording (CORROBORATE AT BUILD). His body was buried in the church of San Luigi dei Francesi, the French national church in Rome, where a memorial plaque marks his tomb. T5: Bastiat's death was noted respectfully across French journalism, including in newspapers that had opposed him politically; Cobden published a tribute in England calling him 'the most illustrious of the Free-Traders on the Continent.' Economic Harmonies was published in its incomplete state in 1850, then re-issued in expanded form (with additional fragments) by his friend Prosper Paillottet in 1851. The pattern of his life -- huge public output compressed into the last five years, dying young with the positive treatise unfinished -- became a template for how classical liberals told the Bastiat story ever after (Hazlitt's introduction to the 1964 edition dwells on it; Sowell mentions it in his memoir). Further rungs: San Luigi dei Francesi is a landmark church in the Piazza Navona area of Rome, famous also for holding three Caravaggio paintings of the life of St Matthew (1599-1600); Bastiat's tomb there is a small quiet plaque, not a large monument.

name: Physiocrats and classical liberals: Bastiat's inheritance
scope: Where Bastiat fits in the French economic-thought tradition. T1: 18th-century France produced its own economic-reform tradition BEFORE the classical liberals -- the PHYSIOCRATS, led by Francois QUESNAY (1694-1774), physician to Louis XV, and Anne-Robert-Jacques TURGOT (1727-1781), briefly controller-general of finance under Louis XVI. T2: Quesnay's 1758 Tableau economique was the first attempt to trace the CIRCULAR FLOW of wealth through an economy; his central (and later refuted) claim was that only AGRICULTURE produces new net wealth ('produit net') -- manufacturing and commerce merely transform it. From this the Physiocrats coined 'laissez faire, laissez passer' -- 'let it be done, let it pass' -- as the policy motto arguing government should not obstruct trade. T3: TURGOT, as controller-general 1774-76, actually tried to abolish internal grain-trade restrictions, guild monopolies, and forced labor (the corvee); the reforms were reversed under noble pressure, and his fall in 1776 is a canonical case of political-economy reform blocked by concentrated interests -- prefiguring public-choice analysis by 200 years. T4: JEAN-BAPTISTE SAY (1767-1832) was the bridge from the Physiocrats to Bastiat. Say's 1803 Traite d'economie politique gave the French version of Adam Smith and formulated what came to be called SAY'S LAW ('supply creates its own demand' -- more precisely, the products offered on a market create the purchasing power that buys other products). Say's Law would be attacked by Keynes and defended by the Austrians (Hutt, Rothbard); it remains contested. Bastiat cites Say constantly. T5: Bastiat's place in the lineage -- he inherits from the Physiocrats their free-trade instinct and from Say his systematic classical-liberal framework, and adds his own gift for VIVID EXAMPLES that made the arguments popularly accessible. The line runs Quesnay -> Turgot -> Say -> Bastiat -> (via Menger 1871 and the Austrian school) -> Mises -> Hayek -> Rothbard -> the modern Austrian school. Further rungs: 'laissez faire' is a FRENCH phrase, from the Physiocrats, not English; the story of the merchant Le Gendre answering Colbert's question 'What should we do to help you?' with 'Laissez-nous faire' ('Leave us alone') is the traditional origin, though the phrase's spread through economic writing is via the Physiocrats c. 1750-60.

name: Bastiat inside Mises's Human Action
scope: How the Austrian tradition explicitly built on Bastiat. T1: LUDWIG VON MISES (1881-1973) is the central figure of 20th-century Austrian economics; his 1949 English magnum opus Human Action systematized the whole Austrian framework (praxeology, subjective value, monetary theory, calculation problem, ABCT). Mises knew and cited Bastiat throughout his career. T2: in Human Action Mises praises Bastiat's Sophismes economiques as 'brilliant' and treats the seen/unseen method as a foundational precursor to his own approach; the broken-window fallacy appears in Mises's discussion of the errors of Keynesian aggregate-demand reasoning. Bastiat is one of the classical liberals Mises names as anticipating the Austrian critique of state-directed economies. T3: in Mises's earlier German-language work Nationaloekonomie (1940, the German precursor to Human Action) and in his 1920 paper 'Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth' (the paper that founded the socialist-calculation debate), Bastiat is not the primary source but the CLASSICAL LIBERAL LINEAGE Mises inherits and extends. Mises's method (praxeology -- reasoning from the axiom of purposive human action) is more technically formal than Bastiat's plain journalism, but the substantive conclusions overlap heavily. T4: HAYEK (Mises's student, 1899-1992) rarely cites Bastiat directly but works in the same tradition. HAYEK'S 1945 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' is the deepest theoretical statement of the point Bastiat's positive theory (in Harmonies economiques) had gestured toward -- that market prices communicate dispersed knowledge no central planner can hold. When Sowell later writes Knowledge and Decisions (1980), he is fusing Hayek's 1945 essay with the Bastiat method of concrete example. T5: MURRAY ROTHBARD (1926-1995) is the most explicit modern extender -- his 1970 Man, Economy, and State restates Bastiat regularly; his Rothbard Reader (posthumous, 2016) includes Bastiat-praise essays; his history of economic thought (An Austrian Perspective, 2 vols, 1995) devotes a full chapter to Bastiat as a genuine classical-liberal genius rather than the merely popular pamphleteer Schumpeter had dismissed him as. Further rungs: THOMAS DILORENZO, JEFFREY TUCKER, and JOSEPH SALERNO in the modern Mises Institute have written extensively on Bastiat; the Institute keeps all major Bastiat texts in print in English.

name: Broken window applied to Katrina and 9/11: modern misuses
scope: Where Bastiat's method exposes 21st-century commentary. T1: on September 14, 2001, three days after the World Trade Center attacks, the New York Times columnist PAUL KRUGMAN published a column titled 'Reckonings; After the Horror' arguing that the terrorist attacks 'could even do some economic good' by prompting rebuilding spending. The column drew immediate broken-window-fallacy critique from classical-liberal economists (Don Boudreaux, Russell Roberts, and others) invoking Bastiat directly. T2: after HURRICANE KATRINA (August 29, 2005), similar 'disaster stimulus' claims proliferated -- that Katrina would boost Gulf-region GDP through rebuilding, that the destruction would 'churn' the economy. Bastiat's move -- the resources spent rebuilding were resources NOT spent on their previous use; the destroyed capital (homes, businesses, infrastructure) is a real UNSEEN loss -- was repeatedly invoked in critique. T3: CASH FOR CLUNKERS (formally the Car Allowance Rebate System, CARS Act signed June 24, 2009) provided $3 billion in vouchers ($3,500-$4,500 per trade-in) for owners to scrap older vehicles and buy new fuel-efficient ones. The program destroyed 690,114 used cars (final DOT figure). SEEN: 690,114 new-car sales in a recession. UNSEEN: 690,114 used vehicles removed from the used-car market, raising prices for lower-income buyers who could not afford new; the DESTRUCTION of vehicles that still had useful working life. T4: the DEEPER MOVE Bastiat's method exposes -- in all three cases (9/11, Katrina, Cash for Clunkers), the visible measured 'economic activity' (rebuilding, replacement) is treated as NET GAIN, when it is actually MOVEMENT of resources from their previous use to the new use, plus the pure loss of the destroyed original capital. This is the 'GDP measures what is spent, not what is destroyed' problem -- GDP as an indicator can rise from destruction and rebuilding, but real WEALTH has fallen. T5: modern classical-liberal writers who have made this argument prominently: Don BOUDREAUX (Cafe Hayek blog, numerous columns 2001-present), Russell ROBERTS (EconTalk podcast, The Price of Everything), THOMAS SOWELL (Basic Economics, chapter on saved-and-lost), STEVEN LANDSBURG (The Armchair Economist 1993). Bastiat's original 1850 essay is the source they all cite. Further rungs: WAR-AS-STIMULUS is the same fallacy applied at scale (that WWII 'ended the Great Depression' -- true that measured GDP rose, false that Americans' consumption did; household consumption FELL 20%+ during the war years); this is Robert Higgs's argument in Depression, War, and Cold War (2006).

name: The Liberty Fund Collected Works: Bastiat in modern English
scope: The definitive modern edition. T1: for most of the 20th century, English readers of Bastiat depended on the FEE editions (Russell 1950 The Law; de Huszar 1964 Selected Essays; Goddard 1964 Economic Sophisms) -- excellent for their day but incomplete; large portions of Bastiat's correspondence, journalism, and Assembly speeches had never been translated. T2: LIBERTY FUND (an Indianapolis-based classical-liberal educational foundation, founded 1960 by Pierre F. Goodrich) undertook a complete English edition of Bastiat's works starting in the 2000s under the general editorship of Jacques de Guenin, Jean-Claude Paul-Dejean, and (for the English) David M. Hart. T3: the resulting Collected Works of Frederic Bastiat runs to a projected six volumes (some sources say seven), of which the first (2011, The Man and the Statesman: The Correspondence and Articles on Politics) and second (2012, The Law, The State, and Other Political Writings, 1843-1850) and third (2017, Economic Sophisms and 'What is Seen and What Is Not Seen') are complete, with volumes four through six covering Free Trade, Harmonies economiques, and remaining Sophisms and correspondence continuing to appear. T4: the Liberty Fund edition provides SCHOLARLY apparatus none of the earlier translations had -- full introductions locating each essay in the French context, glossaries of French political figures Bastiat sparred with, cross-references to when each Sophism appeared in French journals, and modern English translations that RESTORE passages older translations had softened or omitted. T5: the CW project matters because Bastiat's actual sustained arguments (like the six-month Proudhon debate on interest, or the collected Cobden correspondence) had been unavailable to English readers in full for over 150 years; the modern Austrian revival (Rothbard's Mises Institute, the George Mason Bastiat-adjacent economists Boudreaux and Roberts) draws on this newly-available material. Further rungs: DAVID M. HART, the CW's English editor, has also maintained the Online Library of Liberty (oll.libertyfund.org), a free online archive of classical-liberal texts including all the Bastiat volumes -- meaning any curious 21st-century reader with internet access can read Bastiat's complete works in English at no cost.

name: The universal reach: Bastiat as economics-writing's method
scope: The synthesis ladder that closes the pillar. T1: what makes Bastiat DIFFERENT from most classical-liberal writers is his commitment to PLAIN PROSE aimed at the general reader -- neither the mathematical style of continental theorists like Cournot (whose 1838 Recherches used calculus to model demand curves) nor the abstract-philosophical style of some Austrians. Bastiat wrote so a farmer could follow. T2: the specific METHOD Bastiat pioneered has three parts: (i) START with a concrete SCENE (a shopkeeper's window, a French Chamber debate, a proposed railway) that captures the argument to be examined; (ii) STATE the opposing view in its STRONGEST form (steelmanning, 175 years before the term); (iii) trace the UNSEEN consequences the opposing view has hidden. This three-part discipline is what makes his work still readable and still assignable to schoolchildren. T3: the method's TRANSPORTABILITY -- because it does not depend on formal apparatus, it can be applied to any economic argument in any language in any decade. Hazlitt applied it to New Deal policies in 1946; Sowell to affirmative action and welfare policy from the 1970s; Boudreaux to tariffs in the 2010s; George Will and P.J. O'Rourke to political rhetoric across careers. The method scales. T4: the LIMITS of the method -- it is not a substitute for formal economic analysis of monetary policy (that requires Menger, Mises, Hayek, and the technical Austrian apparatus), of capital theory (Bohm-Bawerk), or of public choice (Buchanan-Tullock). Bastiat's genius is at the level of PUBLIC ECONOMIC ARGUMENT -- of teaching a citizen how to see through the standard sophisms about tariffs, subsidies, make-work, and destruction-as-stimulus. His method is the FIRST tool in a classical-liberal citizen's kit, not the only one. T5: the pattern this ENTIRE pillar has traced -- man from 1801 Mugron, working alone on a family farm, teaches himself Adam Smith and Say, watches the 1848 revolutions from Paris, spends the last five years of his 49-year life writing pamphlets that demolish the standard bad economic arguments of his day, dies at Christmas 1850 in Rome with his positive theory unfinished, and 175 years later his short essays are still the best introduction to economic reasoning most classical-liberal readers ever encounter. That story, and that method, are what the pillar teaches. Further rungs: the exact list of economists and writers who cite Bastiat as formative -- Hayek, Mises, Rothbard, Hazlitt, Sowell, Friedman, Boudreaux, Roberts, Ron Paul, Ammous, DiLorenzo, Tucker, Salerno, Higgs, Reisman -- is essentially a directory of the modern Austrian-adjacent tradition.
